UNITED NATIONS – TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 2013 – 2015
Executive Summary
This United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) 2014–2015 for the Republic of 
Trinidad and Tobago articulates the inclusive collective determination of the UN system to support the
Government and People of Trinidad and Tobago, as it implements its ‘prosperity for all’ vision.
The UN System together with the Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago (GoRTT) and key 
stakeholders formulated the biennial rolling UNDAF through an inclusive, participatory and consultative 
process. The formulation and drafting process was guided by the UN’s comparative advantage, lessons 
learnt from the previous UNDAF 2008-2011, an analysis of the country’s current challenges and 
alignment with national priorities.
The overarching principles of Human Rights and Gender Equality were used to formulate the UNDAF and 
to identify the TT UNDAF Pillars. Innovation, Governance, Gender Equality and Human Rights including 
strengthening the national statistical system, were highlighted as cross cutting issues. Data collection 
will also be supported by the UN during the UNDAF period. The four areas identified will be supported 
by the GoRTT, key stakeholders and the UN with resources and efforts from 2014-2015. The UNDAF is a 
dynamic document that could be renewed after 2015, updated or adjusted at any time taking into 
account emerging development issues in the Trinidad and Tobago context.
The four UNDAF pillars are:- (i) Poverty Reduction (ii) Health & Well Being (iii) Citizen Security & Gender 
Equality (iv) Food Security and Environment. 
 
In keeping with the UN country programming principles of engagement, emphasis will be placed on
participation and inclusivity in all spheres, applying a human rights-based, gender and child -sensitive
approach paying special attention to the emerging inequalities, as support is provided to policy and 
planning, environmental sustainability, results-based management, capacity development and technical 
assistance.
The implementation strategy will be overseen by a joint steering committee composed of GoRTT 
Permanent Secretaries, the UN Country Management Team and key stakeholders from civil society and 
the private sector. The Minister of Planning and Sustainable Development and the UN Resident 
Coordinator co-chairs the Steering Committee. Four Result Groups representative of the UNDAF pillars, 8

including a Monitoring and Evaluation Team will be responsible for overseeing the effective and efficient 
implementing and monitoring of programmes and activities under UNDAF pillars. The UN Gender 
Theme Group will support the four results groups in ensuring gender equality issues are a core part of 
the UNDAF response and the UN Communication Group together with the Ministry of Planning and 
Sustainable Development Communications Department will communicate the work of the UNDAF 
during implementation.
The monitoring and evaluation framework will be directed by a specific Result group, through annual 
reviews and through a final evaluation. This group will also be responsible for reviewing technical 
support to strengthen the national statistical system. 
1. Introduction
The UNDAF for the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago provides the UN with a tool to enhance direct 
engagement with national partners on the national development agenda. It is a strategic programme 
framework that describes the collective response of the UN system to national development priorities. 
The integrated programming and monitoring framework with country-level contributions enhances UN 
coherence.
The UNDAF takes into account the realities of Trinidad and Tobago as a non OECD, small island 
developing state with a high income status striving to realize the Millennium Development Goals
(MDGs) by 2015. As 2015 also culminates the governing administrative cycle the GoRTT together with 
the UN agreed to develop an inclusive two-year rolling UNDAF.
The UN system based on its comparative advantage offers to support the Government “that through 
creativity, innovation and collaboration, ‘the people of Trinidad and Tobago’1shall prosper together”. 
A multifaceted approach will be utilized by the UN in its development assistance. Focusing on the people 
of Trinidad and Tobago, the UN will deliver creative innovative programmes and strategies for greater 
social inclusion so as to ensure no one is left behind. Technical assistance and capacity building to
enhance governance systems will be provided. The UN will advocate for the implementation and 
monitoring of key international conventions and accelerate the achievement of the MDGs, according to 
international standards and best practices.
Building on the United Nations Charter and the 2012 United Nations General Assembly Quadrennial 
Comprehensive Policy Review (QCPR)2, the UNDAF establishes the commitment of UN agencies to work 
together as one to increase coherence, collaboration and harmonization that will enhance the UN’s 
impact on human rights and development. Since ‘Tackling inequality and being custodians of the 
environment are crucial features of the sustainable development agenda in T&T’ (Senator the Hon. Bhoe 
Tewarie, Human Imagination at Work Forum, 18 Nov 2013). Sustainable development is the underlying 
concept within which this UNDAF has been built.

1.1 Trinidad and Tobago’s Development Challenges
According to 2012 data from the World Bank, Trinidad and Tobago is depicted as a high-income 
developing country ranking 67th out of 187 countries with a Human Development Index (HDI) of 0.760
and an economy that relies heavily on the energy sector. While positive advancement towards the 
achievement of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) is evident, there have been challenges along 
the way in the efforts towards sustainability of the environment, diversification of the economy and the 
enhancement of the social sector. In order to address these burgeoning challenges associated with 
sustainability, the Medium Term Policy Framework 2011-2014 (MTPF 2011-2014) highlights the 
Government’s strategies to address sustainable development. Namely the seven interconnected pillars 
for sustainable development are: (1) People-centred Development; (2) Poverty Eradication and Social 
Justice; (3) National and Personal Security; (4) Information and Communication Technologies; (5) A more 
diversified knowledge intensive economy; (6) Good Governance; and (7) Foreign Policy.
Like most SIDS, the nation is faced with a number of simultaneous, interrelated and evolving challenges 
of sustainability which have an impact on the standard of living, achievement of the MDGs and the 
health of individuals especially the most vulnerable. 
Addressing issues on policy and legislation, health, education and awareness, climate change, social 
inclusion rehabilitation, aging population and sustainable development will augment the development 
agenda of Trinidad and Tobago. The GoRTT has economic sustainability as a high priority and some 
measures have been established to realize this. However, heavy dependence on the energy sector, the 
need to diversify the energy mix, food security, addressing the need of the most vulnerable, a green 
economy, innovative financing3, human capital and managed migration can be improved. Hindering the 
creation of sustainability within the society are issues of socio-economic inequality, challenges with 
healthcare delivery, citizen security, gender inequality, inclusive governance, infrastructure and housing. 
The GoRTT completed its 2011 census this year, nevertheless the need to strengthen the Central 
Statistical Office to expedite the computation of data, particularly vital statistics needed for evidence 
based planning is pressing. 
1.2 National Development Priorities 
In the thrust towards sustainable development, the GoRTT has identified five priority areas for focused 
and targeted actionable initiatives, in the Medium Term Policy Framework (MTPF) 2011-2014 Innovation 
for Lasting Prosperity. The five (5) Priority Areas for Sustainable Development are:
(i) Crime and Law and Order
(ii) Agriculture and Food Security
(iii) Health Care Services and Hospitals
(iv) Economic Growth, Job Creation, Competitiveness and Innovation
(v) Poverty Reduction and Human Capital Development
The National Performance Framework 2012-2015 and the Three-Year Public Sector Investment 
Programme 2013-2015 by the GoRTT have been developed to ensure goals are aligned with efforts and

2.1 RESULTS OF THE UNDAF
This UNDAF for Trinidad and Tobago focuses on four broad thematic pillars that enhance and 
complement the national priorities and growth agenda of the GoRTT.
Each pillar has several outcomes towards which efforts of the UN system in partnership with the GoRTT 
and stakeholders will be focused on addressing policy, legal, institutional and capacity gaps, thereby 
advancing the national development agenda, the MDGs and the fulfillment of human rights.12 UNITED NATIONS – TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 2013 – 2015
2.2. Pillar 1: POVERTY REDUCTION
Under this pillar, the UN in partnership with the GoRTT and stakeholders, will target programming in 
support of marginalized communities, youth and poorer populations, so as to ensure no one is left 
behind in the overall development of the country. The two outcomes under this pillar are aimed at 
ensuring the availability of adequate social protection systems and supporting the provision of skills for 
employability to secure decent employment, for youth and men and women from rural poor 
communities.
Key data
The GORTT has adopted “a target to reduce poverty by 2% per annum” (SSIP, 2014 p.51). The most 
recent data indicates poverty levels of 16.7% (2005: Survey of Living Conditions) and 14.8% (2008/09 
Household Budgetary Survey). 
In 2005 GoRTT poverty statistics identified the above mentioned marginalized groups as indigent 
(extremely poor) constituting 1.2 %, and the vulnerable as 9% of the population (SSIP, 2014: 51).
Trinidad and Tobago labour force participation rates vary, in the case of men from 78.3 per cent in 
Chaguanas to 65.7 per cent in Arima, and for women from 68.6 per cent in Tobago to 41.2 per cent in 
Princes Town (Trinidad and Tobago Human Development Atlas 2012)
Poverty eradication is a priority for the GoRTT, indicated in the Medium Term Policy Framework under
Poverty Reduction and Human Capital Development. 
The GORTT further recognizes that constructing “a society free from poverty” requires a variety of 
strategies designed to:
 Create sustainable employment and income generating opportunities;
 Provide appropriate housing solutions;
 Develop and build citizens through traditional and non-traditional life skills education and 
training programmes;
 Reform and restructure social safety net programmes;
 Modernise social service delivery systems; ensuring integration and all that need have access;
and
 Encourage and nurture self-reliant and sustainable communities (SSIP, 2014: 51-52).
Poverty eradication is being addressed through a collective effort by all social sector entities. The 
guiding tenet to realizing this goal is “Helping, Empowering and Transforming Lives” (SSIP, 2014: 52). 
The Ministry of the People and Social Development (MPSD) “is mandated to address the social 
challenges of poverty, social inequality and social exclusion”. The MPSD is responsible for “developing, 
coordinating, monitoring and evaluating social sector policies and programmes to ensure sustainability, 
cultural relevance, and economic viability” (SSIP, 2014: 52), and will take the lead and to work with 
“other key social sector ministries” (and other agencies), to “empower its clientele through 
rehabilitative and skill enhancement initiatives” (SSIP, 2014: 52). 
The collective GoRTT’s programmes look to ensure a focus on women and children living in poverty,
(including adolescent mothers and single headed householders) persons with disabilities, the elderly, 
the poor/indigent, the socially displaced, ex-prisoners, deportees and persons living with HIV and AIDS” 
(SSIP, 2014: 52).13 UNITED NATIONS – TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 2013 – 2015
In Trinidad and Tobago an examination of the unemployment rate by sex reveals that women fare worse 
than men in the labour market and by age cohort those between 15-24 years also face higher unemployment rates compared to the rest of the market.
Key poverty eradication projects are delivered through the MPSD include the Micro Enterprise and 
Training Grant (MEG); Micro Enterprise Loan Facility (MEL); Multi-Purpose Community Based Telecentres (MCBT); and the Regional Micro Project Fund (RMPF) (SSIP, 2014: 52) and RISE UP. These 
projects focus on a sustainable, developmental approach to poverty reduction and eradication. 
Considered in conjunction with the Human Capital Development Programmes delivered through the 
Ministries of Education, Health, and Housing, this approach which focuses on targeting the poor and 
vulnerable is key to realizing and sustaining poverty eradication in Trinidad and Tobago.
The UNDAF Pillar One on Poverty Reduction will address this issue with two outcomes. The first 
outcome proposes Social Protection Floor (ILO Social Protection Floor Recommendations 2012-No.202)
approach as an integrated set of social policies designed to guarantee income security and access to
essential social services for all, paying particular attention to vulnerable groups (children and women) 
and protecting and empowering people across the life cycle. The implementation of nationally defined 
social protection floors is envisaged as an important tool in the framework to eradicate extreme poverty 
and address income inequality in Trinidad and Tobago. 
The Social Protection Floor promotes a two-dimensional strategy for the extension of social security, 
comprising a basic set of social guarantees for all (horizontal dimension) and the gradual and progressive 
realization of higher standards (vertical dimension). In Trinidad and Tobago, there is already an 
intermediary level of social protection coverage; hence the human-rights based social protection floor 
will serve to extend coverage horizontally as a first step to progressive realization of universal, 
integrated and comprehensive social protection systems. The design and implementation of a 
nationally-defined social protection floor would be country-led and followed by country specific 
dynamics incorporating national needs, priorities and resources.
The UN System in partnership with national stakeholders aims to develop basic child and gender 
responsive based social protection package and its sub-components for Trinidad and Tobago. It will 
support the GoRTT to conduct national budget reviews and fiscal space analysis for the social protection 
floor in Trinidad and Tobago. This work will be mainstreamed in proposed national poverty reduction 
strategy.
Additionally, this pillar on poverty reduction will address the need for the development of a functional 
Central Beneficiary Registry which will record all persons who access social services and programmes 
offered by all agencies whose mandates address poverty. The Central Beneficiary Registry, which will be 
the key output from the pilot program to be implemented under this outcome, is intended to eliminate 
much of the existing duplication in resource distribution that characterize the existing system, as a result 
of persons accessing benefits from multiple sources. The increased efficiency and effectiveness brought 
about by this registry would result in greater access to services and benefits by those most in need of 
the services offered (i.e., the most disadvantaged, deprived and vulnerable). UNDAF Outcome 1.1 – By 
2015, all income poor and disadvantaged men and women, boys and girls, have access to effective 
and efficient integrated social protection systems.
Latest statistics from the Central Statistical Office indicates that almost 35% of the total unemployed 
were young people, with youth unemployment rate recorded at 12.1% in 2011. Disaggregated by sex, 14 UNITED NATIONS – TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 2013 – 2015
the female rate was at 16.4% and 9.3% for males. The second approach will build on the expected result 
of Outcome 1.1 and an MOU signed by the UN System with the GoRTT to build capacities of recent 
graduates assigned to the national ‘On the Job Training’ (OJT) Programme. Given the need for a more 
sustainable approach to poverty reduction, capacities of young people, poor rural men and women will 
be built for decent work. Under this outcome the youth will gain work experience which will enhance 
their capacities to function in an international organization. Additionally, rural youth, men and women 
will also gain employability skills. Outcome 1.2 – By 2015, youth including men and women from rural 
poor communities have improved employability skills and sustainable income.
2.3 Pillar 2: HEALTH AND WELL BEING
This pillar focuses on supporting access to quality healthcare service, with particular emphasis on
reproductive health, curbing infant and child under five mortality rates and enhancing the well-being of 
all. Outcome 2.1 - Increased access to quality interventions to improve the health of women, 
newborns, children, adolescents, and adults by 2015. Outcome 2.2 - Increased access to interventions 
to prevent and manage non-communicable diseases and their risk factors.
Key data
The infant mortality rate in 2012 was 18 deaths per 1,000 live births (World Bank, 2012)
The children under 5 mortality rate was at 21/1,000 per live births in 2012 the MDG target of 7.4 per 
1,000 live births is unlikely to be met by 2015. (World Bank, 2012)
The country’s Contraceptive Prevalence Rate is 42.5% in 2006 (GoRTT)
Between 2007 and 2011, 65% of all newly reported HIV infection occurred among the age group 25-49 
years. (HIV/AIDS Unit Office Prime Minister)
The age group 15-24 years accounted for 20% of all new infections from 2007 to 2011. (HIV/AIDS Unit, 
Office Prime Minister)
Adolescent birth rate is 44.9 per 1000 women aged 15-19 (MoH data 2012)
Over the past decade the demographic profile of the country has undergone a marked declining fertility 
rate. The PAHO Health Situation in the Americas Basic Indicators, reflects a rate of 1.8 in 2013 and 
according to the 2011 Census Demographic Report a decrease in the under-15 population, and an 
increase (doubling) of the over-60 age group (1). The crude birth rate increased from 12.9 in 2006 to 
14.37 in 2010, to 14.5 per 1000 population in 2013 (PAHO Health Situation in the Americas Basic 
Indicators, 2013), and the crude death rate fell from 10.57 in 2006 to 8.21 in 2010. With the changing 
age structure of the population, human capacity in terms of labor supply to maintain the aging and 
nonworking population declines, resulting in the need for increased government expenditure to support 
the elderly. This is also posing important challenges to productive sectors which require young workers. 
Despite overall declining fertility rates, some segments of the population, particularly in poorer 
communities have higher fertility rates. In Sangre Grande, the adolescent pregnancy rate is as high as 
75% per 1,000 young women age 15-19. (GoRTT Human Development, Atlas 2012).
Although over 95% of women attend antenatal clinics at least once during their pregnancy and are 
attended by skilled health professionals at delivery, there are avoidable deaths due to pre-eclampsia, 
diabetes, premature labor, and infections. The provisional maternal mortality rate for 2010 depicted by 
the 2012 Trinidad and Tobago Human Development Atlas was 49.5 per 100,000 live births (19), a 
significant reduction from previous years. It is likely that later figures will be more encouraging. 15 UNITED NATIONS – TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 2013 – 2015
Maternal mortality and morbidity are key areas of concern. The UNFPA is currently working with the 
CSO, the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Legal Affairs to strengthen the accuracy and timeliness of 
data. 
Infectious diseases and acute respiratory infections are the leading causes of morbidity in children under 
1 year old. Infant mortality rates have shown a relative decline over the period 2005–2009 with a rate of 
18 per 1,000 live births in 2012. Stillbirths accounted for 19% of infant deaths in 2009 and in that year 
low birth-weight was recorded for 19% of all births. According to UNICEF data for 2011, less than 20% of 
infants are breastfed exclusively for at least six months, despite a rate of 41% for early initiation of 
breastfeeding. The under-5 mortality rate for the last two decades (1990–2009) has consistently 
exceeded 30 deaths per 1,000 live births. The World Bank in 2012 reported Under 5 mortality rate at 21 
per 1000 live births. This is currently being addressed in a targeted manner by the Ministry of Health. 
In 2009, approximately 6% of children under age 5 were underweight, where as 11.9% newborns had 
low birth weight <2500gm. There has also been an increasing trend of overweight children. The five 
leading causes of death for both sexes in the period 1997–2007 were cardiovascular diseases, malignant 
neoplasms, diabetes mellitus, cerebrovascular disease, and external causes of injuries. In 2010, 12% of 
the population was over 60 years, lead causes of morbidity were chronic, non-communicable diseases. 
The population’s principal causes of morbidity and mortality Infectious disease are HIV, TB and vector 
borne diseases such as dengue fever (PAHO/WHO). The incidence of accidents and injuries are among 
the top five causes of death since the 1990s. The main health challenges relate to high incidence and 
prevalence of chronic, non-communicable diseases and their risk factors. Regional and local strategies 
have been developed to effectively address their prevention and to promote healthy lifestyles.
Youth adolescent girls are disproportionately affected by sexually transmitted viral infections including 
HIV. Despite the prevalence of transactional sex particularly amongst young girls and issues of 
adolescent pregnancy, current legislation limits adolescents’ access to Sexual Reproductive Health (SRH). 
Due to stigma and discrimination and current legislation, there are some key populations such as young 
women and men sex workers, including men who have sex with men who are particularly vulnerable to 
HIV and other Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI). 
The Ministry of Health has focused on a number of high priority initiatives including support for Patients’
Rights; construction and upgrade of public health care facilities across the country; empowering the 
population to achieve a healthy lifestyle; integrating SRH services at the primary care level, reversing the 
increasing incidence of chronic non-communicable diseases; accidents and injury; HIV-AIDS and other 
communicable diseases; and transforming mental health. The Ministry of Health is also taking active 
steps to improve health sector responsiveness and has made important interventions to address chronic 
diseases, promote healthier lifestyles and to further improve infant mortality rates, children’s health and
improve collection of health data in a timely manner. 
UN agencies in Trinidad and Tobago have demonstrated exceptional technical competence and 
experience and have mandates to deliver technical cooperation in the two priority outcomes identified 
above. In addition to each agency’s comparative advantage, the UN brings a wealth of international
experience as well as the ability to convene key development partners 4together to address some of the 
challenges the health sector faces and to support Government’s focus on improving a number of areas.
